prompt: Asked for the empty placeholder test files (backend and frontend) to be filled in with real, passing tests rather than left empty.
ai_output: Wrote 15 backend Jest+Supertest tests against an in-memory MongoDB, covering create/edit-lock/delete-lock/report-number-reuse/notify-contractor/status-filtering, and 18 frontend Vitest tests covering the extracted business-rule helper functions plus a component test for the checklist's bulk pass/fail buttons. Extracted duplicated inline logic (edit/delete eligibility, compliance derivation, checklist-fail detection) into a separate helpers file specifically so it could be unit tested independently of any UI.
decision: accepted only after independently running both suites and confirming all 33 tests actually passed
notes: Did not take "the tests should pass" as sufficient - ran them personally on my own machine before considering the task complete.

prompt: Asked for sample inspection report data to demo with, and later needed help creating and troubleshooting a one-off seeding script.
ai_output: Added a seedInspections() function to the shared seed.js file, matching the pattern a teammate had already used for scheduling data, generating realistic sample reports across different statuses and defect severities. When the seeding script failed with a DNS connection error, diagnosed it as the same local-network DNS-SRV-resolution issue already worked around elsewhere in the codebase and added the matching fix.
decision: accepted after independently verifying the actual database state (not just trusting the script's console output)
notes: Insisted on directly querying document counts in MongoDB Atlas to confirm the seed data existed and that no other collections had been affected, rather than trusting the script printed success.

prompt: Reported that a teammate's data appeared to be missing from the Scheduling feature after applying a patch, and asked whether the AI's changes had caused it.
ai_output: Clarified that it had no network access to the team's live database at all and could not have altered it directly. Walked through a diagnostic process (checking actual document counts via a script using the project's own database credentials) which showed the teammate's data was, in fact, still present - the issue was a misunderstanding, not real data loss.
decision: accepted the AI's explanation of its own access limitations, but independently verified the data was intact via the diagnostic script rather than just accepting reassurance
notes: Important moment: did not simply trust the AI's claim that nothing was deleted - checked the actual database directly before concluding the concern was unfounded.
